newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour may prove wary of EMU, economists predict.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour may prove wary of EMU, economists predict.

text.p: Britain's Labour party is expected to adopt a more Euro-friendly line if it wins the next general election, but leading economists in London's financial district believe it will tread warily towards a single European currency.

That may disappoint Britain's European trading parters and leading figures in the City of London who are hoping Labour will embrace the single currency project and thaw the often frosty relations between the other European Union members and Britain.

"There are many Euro-sceptics in the Labour party...and they would face exactly the same problems as the Conservatives. I would put the chances of Labour taking us into the first wave of EMU as low as five percent," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.

While most economists put the likelihood higher than that -- at around 30 to 40 percent -- most reckoned Labour might simply be too busy in its first term tackling a demanding domestic agenda to deal with the huge demands of embracing the Euro.

"If they wanted to join EMU it would burden them with such a broad range of legislation that there would be very little room left for anything else," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB in London.

For rank and file members of the Labour party who have spent the last 17 years in the political wilderness, the downgrading of domestic policy to a controversial EMU-agenda would be simply unacceptable in a first term of office, analysts said.

Labour has, for example, made tackling unemployment a prime policy goal, and a headlong rush to ensure the UK hits all the convergence criteria may interfere with achieving that aim, based on the experience of France and other European nations.

What's more, Labour would have to sell a pro-EMU policy to a British public and media which still remains hostile to crucial elements of moves towards a single currency, and is deeply aware of Britain's last and damaging flirtation with currency pacts -- the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

"The UK's intellectual and historical background is just very different from Europe. EMU has not evolved in a sensible, pragmatic way but a rather murky and curious way which is just not in tune with British institutions, public opinion and the media," said Nikko's Briscoe.
At Labour's annual conference in the faded seaside town of Blackpool this week Labour was at pains -- much like the Conservatives -- to leave their options firmly open on EMU and a single currency.

Tony Blair, who has revived Labour's support among key electoral groups including the more EMU-friendly middle classes, vowed on Wednesday that he would seek the consent of the British people before taking any decision on joining a single currency.
Even if, as seems unlikely, Labour decided it wanted to be in the first wave of single currency entrants, the timetable would be extremely demanding.

"It would probably take at least a year for the party to fully convince themselves it was the thing to do and then they would have to plan and organise a referendum," said Steve Hannah, economist at IBJ International. On such a timetable, meeting the 1999 EMU start date would be tough, he added.
